https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.title: ‘Scientists lose our credibility when we become climate activists’
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.text:
A Cambridge climate scientist has called on his colleagues to step back from activism, arguing that they risk undermining the science to fit the politics.
Writing in the journal NPJ Climate Action, Ulf Büntgen, professor of environmental systems analysis, said that he was “concerned by climate scientists becoming climate activists.”
He wrote: “An ever-growing commingling of climate science, climate activism, climate communication and climate policy, whereby scientific insights are adopted to promote pre-determined positions, not only creates confusion among politicians, stakeholders and the wider public, but also diminishes academic credibility.” He added that they risked making climate change a “dogmatic ersatz religion for the wider public”.
He added: “While I have no problem with scholars taking public positions on climate issues. I see potential conflicts when scholars use information selectively or over-attribute problems to anthropogenic warming, and thus politicise climate and environmental change.
“Without self-critique and a diversity of viewpoints, scientists will ultimately harm the credibility of their research and possibly cause a wider public, political and economic backlash.”
His article has split the community. Although some have been supportive others, he said, had not. Michael Mann, professor of earth and environmental science at the University of Pennsylvania, described the argument, which is a regular point of discussion among climate scientists, as “superficial, naive and rather mendacious”, arguing that, given what they knew, scientists had a duty to engage in public debate.
Professor Emily Shuckburgh, director of Cambridge Zero, the University of Cambridge’s climate change initiative, said: “It certainly isn’t our role to advocate for any particular policy, nevertheless it is a source of great personal sadness that our now decades-old warnings regarding the risks posed by climate change have too often been ignored.”
Büntgen maintained that, in his view, there was a risk that the field could be damaged by a public perception that scientists were invested in their results.
He also said that scientific journals had more interest in eye-catching “records” and that this had led to bias. “If I submit a paper where we have such a strong warming trend, something unprecedented, really sticking out, they want that. Do they want a boring study showing it’s flat?” he said.
“I’m a scientist,” he told The Times. “There is no doubt that reducing greenhouse gases is a good thing, but that is not a justification to say we ignore the principles of research.”
Büntgen pointed to his own field, paleoclimatology, in which he felt that scientists had spoken with greater certainty than was warranted. Tree-ring chronologies can be used to reconstruct past temperatures on a millennial timescale, leading to evidence that we now have record-breaking temperatures compared with the past 2,000 years.
He published a paper this week arguing that last summer was the hottest in the northern hemisphere in 2,000 years. However, he said, because trees grow in the summer and the southern hemisphere is mainly ocean, similar data sets have been incorrectly used to argue that the global average annual temperature is record-breaking, when in fact, as in his research, the evidence can only back the statement that the northern hemisphere’s summer temperature is record breaking.
He singled out the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, which synthesises climate data, for a tendency to “overstate scientific understanding of the rate of recent anthropogenic warming relative to the range of past natural temperature variability over 2,000 and even 125,000 years”.
His co-author, Professor Jan Esper, from Johannes Gutenberg University in Germany, said the implications of their research were still scary, but agreed that their job was to only to present the data. “My hope is to move things forward. That we change our energy consumption. But that’s a political question. We are not politicians, we are climate scientists, we should just report as accurately as possible how the situation is. I don’t think we should be activists. But it’s very, very concerning.”
However, Friederike Otto, senior lecturer in climate science at Imperial College, said that Büntgen’s intervention was unhelpful. “Of course science needs to be open when it comes to the outcomes of the studies, but I see no evidence in the scientific community that this is not the case. And he provides none.
“My biggest problem with his piece [in Nature] is that he claims that activism and science are merging. But he never defines what he means with either. If you do not define what you are talking about, of course you can claim anything and nobody can contradict you. But that is exactly what activism does, it is not science.”
Büntgen disagreed. Pointing to the tree-ring data, he said that for the field to be taken seriously it needed to be very clear about the role of science in the conversation. “If we don’t distinguish clearly scientific facts from speculation, and at the end it turns out that it is not correct, what is the credibility of science then?
“I’m afraid that now scientists and activists are becoming all the same. And that is not good for science. In the mid to long term, if we lose our standards then the climate deniers and sceptics, they all have us. You have to be very careful.”

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/education/ar.title: Tube staff inaction led passengers to flee through windows
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/education/ar.subtitle: Investigators found that poor communication contributed to passengers panicking when their Northern Line carriage began to fill with smoke last year
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/education/ar.text:
Tube passengers broke out of a train when Transport for London staff failed to respond to reports of a fire, a report has concluded.
Commuters smashed windows on the Northern Line train to get out after they saw smoke and smelt burning ­inside their carriages in May last year.
The emergency line was pulled, bringing the northbound train to a halt as it left ­Clapham Common at 5.42pm on May 5. Two carriages were inside the tunnel and four were beside the platform.
The Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB) reported that the train doors were kept closed, prompting about 100 of the 500 or so passengers to make their own escape. At first people used doors between the carriages to get on to the platform. Others escaped through smashed windows.
The RAIB said it found that passengers “perceived a significant risk from fire” and became “increasingly alarmed when the doors remained closed”. It added that passengers “did not receive suitable information or see any effective action from London Underground staff” during the incident.
The report said workers had not been provided with the “procedures or training needed to effectively identify and manage incidents where passenger ­behaviour can rapidly escalate”.
The lessons of a similar incident at Holland Park in 2013 had not been ­applied by Transport for London, it added.
Andrew Hall, chief inspector of rail accidents, said staff did not fully appreciate the emerging safety risk when passengers became increasingly anxious.
“When passengers did not receive suitable information about the nature of the incident and the actions they should take, nor see action they would have expected to be taken, they turned to desperate measures,” he added.
The report said there had been communication failures between station staff and the customer service manager. There was a delay of more than four minutes before an assistant on the platform got permission to release the doors. The driver could not open them safely because carriages were in the tunnel.
Hall said after the RAIB investigated a similar incident at Holland Park, “for a number of years that incident was used as an example to train staff. However, it was subsequently removed from the training syllabus and since then knowledge of the lessons learnt may have begun to fade. This incident demonstrates that learning from past operational incidents needs to be retained.”
No major injuries were reported, ­although some passengers had serious wounds.
Nick Dent, the London Underground director of customer operations, apologised for the distress caused to passengers. “We are making good progress on the recommendations from the RAIB,” he added.
“However, it was subsequently removed from the training syllabus and since then knowledge of the lessons learnt may well have begun to fade. This incident again demonstrates that learning from past operational incidents needs to be retained by organisations.”

image.caption: Passengers broke windows and tried to force open doors to get out of the train during the incident in May last yearRAIB/UNPIXS

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.title: Deep-sea mining ‘one of stupidest ideas ever’, says marine biologist
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.subtitle: Sylvia Earle says putting unique creatures and ecosystems on the seabed at risk is absurd
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.text:
Opening up the oceans for deep-sea mining is one of the “stupidest ideas” imaginable, according to an eminent marine biologist.
Sylvia Earle, 88, an American who leads the field of conservation in terms of experience with the likes of Sir David Attenborough and Dame Jane Goodall, said the prospect of putting unique creatures on the seabed at risk was “absurd”.
Deep-sea mining, which the UK opposes, would mean machines extracting metals from polymetallic nodules and manganese crusts. The Metals Company, a Canadian firm, hopes to start commercial mining in the Pacific Ocean this year or next. It argues that doing so would protect habitats on land, such as Indonesian rainforests, because of surging demand for cobalt, nickel and other metals that are vital for technologies used to build electric cars, for example. Norway recently became the first nation to approve commercial deep-sea mining.
However, Earle told The Times’s Planet Hope podcast that opening a new frontier was misguided. “This is wrong on a scale that is unprecedented. We’re talking about systems that are not just thousands of years in the making, or hundreds of thousands of years; we’re talking about millions of years invested. The deeper we go, the less we know, but the more new discoveries we’re finding,” she said.
The seabed targeted by The Metals Company, between Hawaii and Mexico and known as the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, is home to more than 5,000 species, many that are found nowhere else on Earth.
Earle dismissed the idea that mining the oceans was justified by saving terrestrial habitats. “Two wrongs don’t make a right. We’re presuming that it’s OK to go to the deep sea and start bulldozing the ocean floor, disrupting not just the ocean floor, but the water column above. It’s one of the stupidest ideas I’ve ever imagined,” the oceanographer said.
Earle, who in 1968 became the first woman scientist to visit the ocean depths in a submersible vehicle, said she was worried about the current bleaching of coral reefs that is turning colourful coral into white wastelands. It is the fourth mass bleaching since the first event in 1998.
“The bad news is that about half of the coral reefs globally are not just bleaching, they’re gone, since I first started exploring the ocean in the 1950s. Most of the decline has been evident since the 1980s and the pace is picking up,” Earle said, adding that the decline in coral also mattered for the sharks and tuna that rely on those ecosystems.
Earle, who is a vegetarian and was featured in the Netflix documentary Seaspiracy, said people’s diets couldn’t be changed with a hectoring approach. “When you start dictating to people what they should eat, they resist.” A better way, she said, would be for governments to end subsidies that make industrial fishing possible.
“But, most importantly, we need to get people to understand. The biggest disconnect in knowing why you should care,” Earle said.
She said she had lived long enough to see huge changes in the natural world. “David Attenborough, Jane Goodall and I are witnesses of almost a century of change. The whole planet is changing in ways not favourable to us or life. We’re the cause. We can also be the cure.”
When asked what the difference for the oceans would be if President Biden or Donald Trump, who is expected to boost offshore drilling for oil and gas, won the United States election, Earle said: “I don’t think I have to name names. It’s pretty obvious we have the most stark choice we’ve ever had about caring for the future.”

image.caption: Sylvia Earle, a pioneering scientist, claims the argument from industry that ocean mining would protect habitats on land is misguidedKIMBERLY WHITE/GETTY IMAGES

https://www.thetimes.com/article/energy-.title: Energy price cap set to fall again
https://www.thetimes.com/article/energy-.subtitle: Analysts expect consumers to pay £500 less per year than in July 2023
https://www.thetimes.com/article/energy-.text:
Household energy bills are expected to fall to their lowest in two years from July, offering relief for squeezed households.
Analysts at Cornwall Insight, the consultancy, expect energy regulator Ofgem to reduce the annual price cap by £116 to £1,574 from July when it gives its latest update on May 24. It will mean an average household on a default tariff pays £500 per year less than in July last year, when it was £2,074.
The cost of keeping the lights and heating on will, however, still be hundreds of pounds more than before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, which caused wholesale gas and oil prices to spike.
Dr Craig Lowrey, Cornwall Insight’s principal consultant, said the latest projections offered more relief to bill payers after April’s reduction. He added: “Of course, we must recognise lower prices don’t erase all the problems. The very fact we are still seeing bill levels which are hundreds of pounds above pre-crisis levels underscores the ongoing challenges faced by households.”The forecast cap is slightly higher than the £1,560 the group had previously predicted for July, after energy prices rebounded from February’s 30-month low as fears grew of new disruption to energy supplies arising from the Israel-Hamas conflict. Brent crude oil now costs around $83 a barrel, from a high of $112 in the summer of 2022, and natural gas has fallen by 90 per cent from record peaks reached in the months after the invasion of Ukraine.Cornwall Insight has forecast that the price cap will rise slightly at October’s three-monthly Ofgem review before falling again in January 2025. The annual cap was set at £1,137 when it was introduced in 2019 in an effort to prevent energy companies from overcharging customers by capping the amount a supplier can charge per unit of gas or electricity. Ofgem announced a detailed review of the cap earlier this year that would make significant changes to the way it was calculated, in particular to the daily standing charge which costs a typical consumer several hundred pounds a year even before any gas or electricity is used.Lowrey said: “While the cap is certainly not the ticket back to long-term energy bill affordability, Ofgem’s review could pave the way for fairer, more efficient energy bills. However, given the breadth of reforms being considered by the regulator, it is worth remembering that such changes will inevitably lead to trade-offs.”
The gas crisis that broke out in the aftermath of Vladimir Putin’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 led to the collapse of a string of energy companies which could not cover soaring wholesale prices. The government was prompted to intervene and subsidise household bills through the energy price guarantee, limiting a typical bill payer to what was still a record high of £2,500 a year.
Alastair Douglas, chief executive at TotallyMoney, the credit data company, said: “Not long ago, there were almost 50 energy firms fighting for customers, offering price-cap-busting deals for those willing to switch. But now, six suppliers dominate 70 per cent of the market, meaning competition has bottomed out, and the price cap has essentially become a price fix.”
